lines.text: Endless grassland, nomad herders and the largest land empire the world has ever seen. This is the story of Mongolia, from the Xiongnu to today.
More than two thousand years ago, the Xiongnu built a nomad empire on the steppe, and their horsemen threatened Han China for centuries.
In the twelfth century a boy named Temujin was born. As Genghis Khan he would unite the tribes and lead them to conquer half a continent.
His third son, Ogedei, would become the second Great Khan and push the conquests deep into China, Russia and Eastern Europe.
From those days, the Mongols have held Naadam, the summer games of wrestling, archery and horse racing, still the country's greatest festival.
In 1206 the tribes proclaimed Genghis their ruler, and the Mongol Empire was born. It would stretch from Korea to Eastern Europe.
His grandson Kublai Khan would conquer the Song, found the Yuan dynasty of China, and, it is said, welcome Marco Polo to his court.
On the steppe, Karakorum became the capital of the empire, where envoys came from across the known world.
Soon after Genghis died, the Secret History of the Mongols told his life for his family. It is the oldest surviving work in the Mongolian language.
Kublai sent two great fleets to conquer Japan, in 1274 and 1281. Samurai and storms, the divine winds, drove both away.
In 1368 the Yuan fell in China, and the Mongol court went home to the steppe as the Northern Yuan.
In 1585 the monastery of Erdene Zuu was built from the ruins of Karakorum, as Tibetan Buddhism took hold among the Mongols.
A generation later Zanabazar was born, a Buddhist leader whose golden statues are counted among the finest art of Mongolia.
In 1639 a monastery camp was founded that moved across the steppe for a century and more, before it settled. It is today's capital, Ulaanbaatar.
In the late Qing years, the Bogd Khan, Mongolia's religious leader, was born. He would lead its break with China.
Damdin Sukhbaatar, born in 1893, would lead the revolution of 1921. The great square of the capital bears his name.
In 1911, as the Qing dynasty fell, Mongolia declared its independence from China.
Ten years later, Sukhbaatar's revolutionaries, backed by Soviet troops, took power and made Mongolia a Soviet ally.
In 1924 the Mongolian People's Republic was declared, the second communist state in the world after the Soviet Union.
In the purges of the late thirties, about thirty thousand people were killed, many of them Buddhist monks, and the monasteries were emptied.
In 1968 Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh was born. He would become president in 2021.
In 1990 young Mongolians gathered in the freezing squares and peacefully brought communist rule to an end. Democracy had come.
And in 2013 the Oyu Tolgoi mine opened in the south Gobi, one of the largest copper and gold mines in the world.
The empire is long gone, but the steppe, the horses and the spirit of the nomads remain.
